text: Every chapter in this course has quietly done the same thing: stated a speedup, then immediately qualified it. This lesson makes that habit explicit as a five-point checklist you can apply to any claim you hear about quantum advantage — including the ones in this very course.

Rule one: compare against the best known classical algorithm, not a convenient strawman — beating trial division isn't a benchmark of Shor's algorithm, beating the General Number Field Sieve is. Rule two: be precise about what's being counted. Saying Grover's algorithm needs root N steps is true only if step means one oracle query — and each oracle call is itself a quantum circuit, potentially with many gates, which isn't free to build.

Rule three: account for the real hardware gap. Shor's algorithm is polynomial-time and mathematically sound, and still not a practical threat to RSA-2048 today — the widely cited Gidney and Ekerå estimate puts the requirement at roughly 20 million noisy qubits and about 8 hours, and current hardware is nowhere near that scale. An honest benchmark separates asymptotically superior from deployable this year, and says which one it's claiming.

Rule four: asymptotic superiority isn't the same as superiority at the sizes that matter — a classical linear scan can simply be faster in practice at small N, even though it's worse asymptotically. Rule five: state the assumptions and error model explicitly — Deutsch-Jozsa and Simon's algorithm both assume a promise real-world data never comes guaranteed with. Re-reading Chapters 1 through 6 with this checklist shows the course was already doing exactly this, lesson by lesson.
Next lesson puts Grover's algorithm's real, verified numbers next to classical search's real numbers, side by side, and applies this exact checklist to the comparison.
